extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, literary critics, and researchers of humor/theory of wit
extracted.subtask_description: Close theoretical analysis of the psychological mechanisms that produce comic pleasure and wit (Freudian account), identifying distinct species (situation, expectation, imitation, caricature, unmasking, speech) and how wit intersects with the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification expenditure vs normal expenditure (general source of comic pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic pleasure originates in a comparison between two energy expenditures—identification expenditure (Einfühlungsaufwand) and normal expenditure—rapidly following one another and referring to the same function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pleasure arises from the difference between these expenditures. This comparison may be produced by identification with another person or by changes within one's own psychic processes. Keep in mind that the feeling of superiority is not essentially related to comic pleasure: the comparison and resulting difference of expenditure is the key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of Situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic produced when outer influences produce a difference in expenditure (either in ourselves via identification or in our own psychic processes) so that we judge that, placed in the same situation, we would have acted the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on relation of the individual to an often overpowering external world (social conventions, bodily needs). Examples: a person engaged in a demanding activity disturbed by sudden pain or excremental need; the contrast between his former energetic state and the minimal remaining psychic activity after disturbance. The comic is drawn from the situation rather than the person’s inherent qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of Expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic that arises from our relation to anticipated future events: expectation entails a quantitatively determined expenditure (motor preliminaries, sensory tension) which, when disappointed, leaves a surplus or mismatch discharged as laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples include preparing to catch a ball and overreacting when it is lighter than expected, or lifting an apparently heavy basket which proves hollow. Expectation expenditure includes motor preparations and sensory tension; disappointment reduces required expenditure leading to comic effect. Physiological evidence cited (Pavlov's salivary experiments) supports measurable expectation expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing comic by exaggerating a particular feature of an exalted person/object, rendering that feature prominent and thereby degrading the exalted whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caricature isolates one comic feature from the whole picture; this isolation spreads the comic effect over the entire image. The exalted must not force reverence (otherwise caricature fails). Caricature can falsify reality (exaggerate a non-comical trait) without essentially impairing the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making oneself comical intentionally (shamming)
rubrics_metrics.description: One can purposely produce comical elements in oneself (appear awkward or stupid) by complying with the comparison condition that leads to a difference in expenditure, yet this does not necessarily create contempt or superiority in observers if the sham is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional shamming can even secure admiration; when the audience knows the actor is only pretending, the feeling of superiority in the observer does not arise. Use of deliberate self-degradation is a technique for producing comic pleasure distinct from genuine incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical jokes and transferring into comic situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Making another person comical by placing or transferring them into situations where, regardless of personal qualities, they become comic because of human dependence on external circumstances (social factors, bodily needs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be real (practical jokes: causing a person to fall, exploiting credulity) or feigned (speech/play). Practical jokes exploit vulnerability and are effective because everyone is defenseless against being made comical in this way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as comic source
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation yields strong comic pleasure, especially when faithful; the comic arises because perfect similarity reduces the need for new expenditure of understanding and suggests mechanical repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson's account: the laughable is the human that reminds us of a machine. Freud reframes this via expenditure: total agreement/deceptive imitation makes no new expenditure necessary, leading to relief and discharge via laughter. Imitation is linked more to the comic of expectation than to comic of situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody, travesty, and degradation (methods of producing comic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody and travesty degrade the exalted by replacing attributes, speech, or actions with lowly equivalents, thus destroying uniformity and producing comic effect by degradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods act against figures who command authority/respect; they operate by reducing psychic 'greatness' (expressed by added innervation) and thereby remove the added expenditure, leading to comic pleasure. They differ in mechanism from caricature but share the degradation function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unmasking (revealing automatic psychic processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unmasking exposes persons who have assumed dignity/authority as ordinary humans by revealing the monotonous psychic automatism and dependence on bodily needs behind their achievements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the fashionable lady whose true labor-cry exposes human frailty, or anecdotes revealing a marriage agent’s venal motives. Unmasking can serve as a façade for wit; some cases may be classified as comic story rather than pure witticism. Unmasking both degrades and discloses hidden psychic automatism, producing comic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsense-wit and the meeting of wit and comic
rubrics_metrics.description: When wit uses modes of thinking common to the unconscious (faulty thinking), it may present as nonsense to the conscious critic but produce comic pleasure in the third person; thus wit and comic can overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit’s technique of giving free play to unconscious modes (faulty thinking, displaced or juxtaposed thoughts) can appear as comic because the foreconscious comparison of the expressed form to its correct form creates a difference in expenditure. Distinguish cases where wit remains non-absurd (no comic effect) from those where wit employs faulty thinking and thereby yields comic impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faulty thinking technique in wit (technical guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit often uses 'faulty thinking'—modes of unconscious thought—to achieve pleasure; it may disguise such faulty thinking with a semblance of logic or present it as innocent indirect expression to avoid criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If faulty thinking is disguised (e.g., by semblance of logic or retained indirect expressions), the critic will not protest; undisguised faulty thinking invites rejection. Examples: stories that juxtapose multiple mutually exclusive but individually plausible motives (borrowed kettle), producing a nonsensical yet humorous effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison as a source of comic (difference in abstraction expenditures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic in comparison arises from differences in the abstraction expenditure required by the two items compared; when a serious/strange/intellectually sublime thing is compared to something banal, the former is unmasked as lowly because the abstraction expenditure collapses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic comes from the increased 'niveau' difference of abstraction expenditure, not from mere contrast. Comparison is effective as comic when it is pertinent (shows real agreement) and when it accomplishes a degradation by economizing abstraction expenditure. Comparisons can be witty without comic admixture when they evade degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of Imitation (mechanical repetition and rigidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where repetition, perfect similarity, or machine-like movements in humans (rigidity, professional habits, fixed ideas) produce comic impressions because they suggest an inanimate, mechanical life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson's law: human attitudes/gestures are laughable in proportion as they remind us of a mere machine. Freud reframes it as a failure of expected individual variability requiring less expenditure; examples include two too-similar faces, stereotyped professional mannerisms, and fixed modes of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of Speech (intentional and involuntary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic produced by speech techniques—fusions, modifications, substitutions, condensations, and absurd compositions—distinct from wit, though sometimes overlapping; some speech-comic is intentional (comic nonsense) while other instances are involuntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Wippchen: fusing familiar expressions, substituting grandiose words for banal ones, and producing fluent but platitudinous wording. Distinguish comic speech (purely comic effect) from witty speech (clever allusion or double meaning). Comic speech often relies on stylistic devices that reduce substantive expenditure or produce unexpected, banal substitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative contrast (Lipps' view) and predominance of quantity over quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantitative (not qualitative) contrast—differences in magnitude of expenditure—is primarily the source of comic pleasure; motion and a sense of 'bigness/smallness' underlie many comic phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider expectation expenditure, conceptual mimicry (representation of bigness/smallness), and abstraction expenditure as components that can be reduced to a general sense of 'greater' or 'smaller' investment. Lipps' emphasis helps explain many cases but is too narrow to cover all comic phenomena without supplementation.
